cards.b: Bhakti and Sufism are the main strands of medieval religious life. They shaped language, music and social ideas. UPSC asks for saints, teachings and effects.

Bhakti (devotion) began in the south with the Alvars (Vishnu) and Nayanars (Shiva), between the 6th and 9th centuries, who sang in Tamil and welcomed women and low castes (Andal, Karaikkal Ammaiyar). Texts: Nalayira Divya Prabandham, Tevaram. Later: Shankara’s Advaita (8th c.), Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita, 11th to 12th c.), Madhva (Dvaita), Basavanna’s Lingayat movement (Karnataka, 12th c.; Anubhava Mandapa).

• Ramananda (14th to 15th c.): Rama bhakti; disciples include Kabir and Ravidas.
  • Kabir: nirguna God, attacked idol worship and caste; Bijak.
  • Guru Nanak: one God, equality, langar, sangat.
  • Chaitanya (Bengal): Krishna bhakti, kirtan.
  • Tulsidas (Ramcharitmanas), Surdas, Mirabai, Raskhan.
  • Vallabhacharya (Pushtimarga).

Varkari tradition: Dnyaneshwar, Namdev, Eknath, Tukaram, Janabai; Pandharpur and Vitthal. Sankaradeva (Assam, Ekasarana dharma), Shrimanta Sankardeva’s Namghar and Borgeet. Others: Narsi Mehta (Gujarat), Chandidas (Bengal), Annamacharya (Andhra). Many saints came from low castes and used the vernacular.

Sufism is the mystical stream of Islam, stressing love and union with God. Orders (silsilas): Chishti (Khwaja Muinuddin Chishti at Ajmer; Nizamuddin Auliya in Delhi; Baba Farid), Suhrawardi (Multan, Bahauddin Zakariya), Qadiri, Naqshbandi (Sirhindi, who opposed Akbar’s liberalism). Practices: khanqah, sama (music), langar. Chishtis kept away from the state; Suhrawardis accepted it.

Both movements used local languages: Kabir and Tulsi in Hindi, Dnyaneshwar in Marathi, Sufis in Dakhni and Hindavi (Amir Khusrau, Baba Farid in Punjabi). The Chishtis of Ajmer and Delhi attracted Hindu and Muslim devotees. Sufi poets such as Jayasi (Padmavat) and Rahim. Qawwali and bhajan, Kabir panth and Sikhism came from them. Both rejected rigid orthodoxy.

They challenged caste, ritual and priestly control; spread vernacular literature; gave women a voice (Mirabai, Lalla Ded). They brought communities closer and helped shape the ganga-jamuni tehzeeb. Yet they did not abolish caste; many movements later formed new sects or castes. Akbar’s sulh-i-kul was nurtured in this air.

Historians (Satish Chandra, Irfan Habib) see Bhakti as a response to a changing society and urban craft groups; Marxists tied it to peasants and artisans. Others (Romila Thapar) view it as a religious expression within a plural society. Scholars debate the term “movement”, as the saints were not organised. On Sufis, Richard Eaton (Sufis of Bijapur) studies state ties.

Kabir’s and Mirabai’s verses are in school books and music. The dargah of Ajmer, with a huge urs, draws all faiths. Pandharpur’s wari draws lakhs. Discussion on communal harmony cites these traditions; recent controversies over dargahs and temples revisit it. The Sikh langar became a symbol of free community kitchens worldwide.

• “Bhakti and Sufi movements promoted social harmony. Discuss.”
  • “Compare the teachings of Kabir and Guru Nanak.”
  • Prelims tip: Alvars = Vishnu; Nayanars = Shiva; Ramanuja = Vishishtadvaita; Basavanna = Lingayat; Chishti = Ajmer, Nizamuddin; Suhrawardi = Multan.
